author: Dividend Sleuth
title: 2 Unsung Champions
text:
The value of the Dividend Champion universe Each month, David Fish produces an updated list of Dividend Champions - companies that have increased dividends for at least 25 consecutive years. Also, his monthly database includes Dividend Contenders (10+ years) and Dividend Challengers (5+ years).
David's list for May 2018 includes 882 companies: 120 Champions, 217 Contenders and 545 Challengers. It's difficult to overestimate David's contribution to investor education. The 30 stocks in my retirement income portfolio are among the 882 on David's list. The portfolio includes 14 Champions, 7 Contenders and 9 Challengers.
It would be a great gift to receive the compendium of information David provides about just one of my portfolio stocks. But, he does it for all 30, updated monthly, available at my fingertips 24/7. As if that's not enough, I view the other 852 companies as potential candidates for my watchlist. And all of this is available from his dripinvesting.org website at no cost.
Longevity is a good start Longevity of dividend increases isn't a perfect vetting mechanism, but it's a good start. When I read about a stock or hear an idea for a stock to study, I begin the vetting process by consulting David's list. If a company has grown its dividend for a minimum of 5 years, it will be on David's list. At a glance, I can check the number of consecutive years of dividend increases, the price and yield at the end of the month just ended, the current quarterly dividend, when it was last increased, and by how much. That's just the beginning.
Also available are data such as these: the ticker symbol, the industry in which the company operates, dividend payment dates and other relevant information about the dividend (ex-dividend dates, etc.), the payout ratio (annual dividend per share divided by annual earnings per share), the trailing 12-month price/earnings ratio, PEG ratio , EPS growth for the past 5 years and projected EPS growth for the next 5 years. David gets some of this data from Finviz .
Many Seeking Alpha dividend investors refer to David's columns that show each company's dividend growth rates for the past 1, 3, 5 and 10 years. David provides the actual dividends paid for each of the previous 19 years. So, including the current year, you have a 20-year dividend history for each of the companies, plus another series of columns that shows the percentage dividend increase for each year. Also, David includes several other dividend growth factors, such as the Chowder Rule , which combines the 5-year dividend growth rate and the current yield.
If a company's 5-year dividend growth rate is an annualized 10% and the current yield is 2.5%, it would have a Chowder Rule number of 12.5. Bob Wells refers to this number as the "Total Dividend Return," or TDR. Bob explains it this way in the first of two 2014 articles about TDR:
"My central focus for this year shifts from yield to Total Dividend Return, TDR. Many Dividend Growth Investors refer to TDR as the "Chowder Rule" in honor of Chowder, a regular contributor here on Seeking Alpha. Under this rule, a stock yielding 4% along with a 5 year Dividend Growth Rate of 8% would produce a total dividend return of 12%. A stock yielding 3% would require higher dividend growth to produce a TDR of 12%. The rule is relaxed a bit for higher yielding/slower growing equities such as utilities, telecoms and MLPs. With this group a total dividend return of 8% is sought."

When I create a watchlist, sometimes I become impatient. I think my target price is too low and I lose interest. On occasion, my loss of interest has meant a lost opportunity to buy shares of a company I think is a great long-term investment. I use Seeking Alpha's portfolio function to create several watchlist portfolios. I check these from time to time to see if one or more of the stocks is approaching the target. I now see a watchlist not as a short-term exercise, but a long process that requires patience. Some brokerage houses offer this capability. I use Custom Stock Alerts to be notified that a stock on a watchlist has reached a target price.
Here's one example: American States Water ( AWR ) is one of six water utilities on David Fish's list of the Dividend Champions. That, in itself, is remarkable. A full 5% of the Champions, 6 of 120, are in one utility sub-sector. AWR almost always receives a premium valuation by the market.
A few years ago, during a dip I was able to pick up some shares at a yield of 3.0%. AWR now yields just 1.79% but I like their business model and their entrepreneurial spirit. They have made good use of federal government contracts (primarily with military bases) to expand beyond their California service region. AWR may be on my watchlist for a long time, but I want to be ready should opportunity arise.

United Bankshares
When the May 2018 list of Dividend Champions was published, UBSI caught my attention because at that time (April 30, 2018), the yield was 4.01%. By May 29, the price had recovered somewhat, dropping the yield to 3.73%.
(Logo from UBSI website )
UBSI is a regional bank with dual headquarters in Charleston, West Virginia and Washington, D.C. UBSI traces its roots to 1839, when the Northwestern Bank of Virginia opened a branch in Parkersburg, Virginia (now West Virginia). United Bankshares became a publicly-traded company in 1987. Since then, the bank has made 31 acquisitions, expanding into the Washington, D.C./Northern Virginia area, as well as parts of Maryland, Ohio and Pennsylvania.
On April 26, 2018, UBSI announced record quarterly earnings of $61.7 million up from $38.8 million for Q1 2017. Diluted earnings per share were $0.59 for the first quarter of 2018 as compared to diluted EPS of $0.48 for Q1 2017.
UBSI has flown "under the radar" on Seeking Alpha. In his 2013 article , Harvard Winters viewed the $25.86 price as 25% overvalued, propped up by a high payout ratio of 70%. At that time, UBSI was in the process of acquiring Virginia Commerce Bancorp.
A full 2 years passed before another SA article featured UBSI, a February 2015 article by Investment Standard, who noted that the 2014 acquisition of Virginia Commerce Bancorp, the largest UBSI acquisition to date, had improved the bank's profitability. The payout ratio had dropped to 66.65%. The stock price was $35.19, the dividend was $1.28 and the yield was 3.64%.
In a June 2015 article , Michael Boyd wrote that UBSI's "dividend history can't be matched," and that "management has consistently invested conservatively with shareholders in mind." The price was $39.52, the dividend was $1.28 and the yield was 3.23%. Michael saw UBSI as expensive relative to its peers:
"UBSI's price/tangible book value currently stands at 2.94, well above the regional bank peer group average. Other measures such as price/sales (6.04) and price/cash flow (19.33) paint a similar picture of relative expensiveness. There are three main reasons shares trade at elevated levels:
1. Relative safety and management stewardship (highlighted above);
2. Marginal outperformance in regards to return on assets/return on equity;
3. Dividend Champion status"
Adam Brown's September 2015 article noted UBSI's 41-year history of dividend increases. The price was $37.13, the dividend was $1.28 and the yield was 3.45%. The payout ratio was around 65%. Adam wrote:
"I believe this is a safe mid­sized bank for any income portfolio....
United Bank has a very healthy balance sheet with a very comfortable 3.45% dividend. This is not a volatile stock and has the scale to make it competitive in its regional market. No stock is perfect, and this one's performance metrics need attention. However, strong cost controls and growing dividend make it worth a look. With the recent pull­backs, this could be the perfect mid­cap bank for an income portfolio looking for a little regional bank exposure."
This September 2015 article was the last SA feature article about UBSI.
(Graph from F.A.S.T. Graphs )
David Fish reports (via Finviz ) trailing 12-month EPS of $2.20 and a current dividend of $1.36, for a payout ratio of 61.82%. The previous 5-year EPS growth rate was 3.2%, but the projected EPS growth rate for the next 5 years is 10.0%. UBSI has an attractive yield of 3.73%, but the dividend growth rate has been low. The 5-year dividend growth rate is 1.3%. Simply Safe Dividends gives UBSI a dividend safety score of 74 (with 50 as average).
UBSI is on my watchlist. I need to do more study, but so far I'm impressed with most of what I've seen. Notice the "choppiness" of the stock's price in the graph below. With patience, should I decide to buy UBSI, I believe I can pick up shares with a dividend yield of at least 4.0%. (My target price to consider making an initial purchase is $34.00, which would equate to a 4.0% yield.) The high yield for each of the past 3 years has ranged from 3.9% to 4.2%.
(Graph from Seeking Alpha )
Sonoco
Sonoco Products Co. has received more attention on Seeking Alpha than UBSI, though not as much as many of the larger, better known Dividend Champions. 17 articles were published from 2009-2017, for an average of less than 2 per year. 3 SON articles have been published so far in 2018.
I like Albert Alfonso's summary in his July 2013 article :
"Sonoco Products seems to be a solid stock for risk-averse investors. The company has a long history of growing its dividend and has mundane, but safe, business model."
In his November 2013 article , Regarded Solutions wrote:
"When we can find a stock that seems to fly under the radar for the most part, but happens to qualify as a dividend at the same time, we should jump on it."
A relatively recent and thorough introduction to SON is available in Charles Gooch's October 2017 article . Charles was attracted to SON's expansion into a broader array of packaging (in light of consumer shifts away from packaged foods) and to SON's conservative balance sheet:
"...in this era of cheap debt that will undoubtedly end eventually, Sonoco hasn't overleveraged its balance sheet. As a matter of fact, the company is in far less debt than its peers."
The most recent SA article about SON has a "green" focus. Jenks Jumps' May 2018 article looks at some of the environmental aspects of this industry and concludes with a positive opinion about Sonoco:
"... Sonoco's potential for growth throughout the world is healthy. Brazil, Thailand, South Africa, the Middle East, Europe, Mexico and Asia are specific targets.
Based on our criteria, Sonoco is also fairly-valued. ... Sonoco updated its 2018 guidance for EPS to a range of $3.22 to $3.32. The forward P/E ratio now hovers around 16. Adjusting for the 3% dividend yield, the forward PEG ratio is approximately 0.80.
Regarding our criteria of clear potential for dividend growth, Sonoco's 35-year track record speaks for itself. ... it explicitly states the plan is to “increase dividends as earnings grow.” Analysts are projecting five-year earnings growth of 6.5% annually.
At the end of the 2018 first quarter, Sonoco's net debt to total capital ratio was 39.2%. Thus, its dividend should not be threatened by an inability to cover debt obligations."
Sonoco began as the Southern Novelty Company in Hartsville, South Carolina, in 1899. SON is still headquartered in Hartsville. It has revenues of $5 billion, with more than 300 operations in 33 countries, serving customers in 85 countries, competing with International Paper ( IP ) and a host of other companies in the packaging industry.
(Logo from Sonoco website )
I do not have a position in Sonoco, but I put it on my watchlist when my wife purchased some shares for her portfolio earlier in 2018. As a manufacturer of packaging, Sonoco is in the materials sector. It's not to be confused with Sunoco ( SUN ), a limited partnership in the energy sector.
At Sonoco's website, you can view some informative slides from a March 2018 presentation to analysts. That presentation indicates this breakdown of 2017 sales:
Consumer Packaging, 42% Paper and Industrial Converted, 37% Protective Solutions, 11% Display Packaging, 10%. (Graph from F.A.S.T. Graphs )
David Fish reports a 5-year dividend growth rate for SON of 5.3%. F.A.S.T. Graphs reflects the BBB+ Standard & Poor's corporate credit rating for SON.
I would prefer a higher credit rating, but the company appears to me to be conservatively managed. I plan to follow this company more closely. I set $50.46 as a target price to consider making an initial purchase. That price equates to a 3.25% yield at the current dividend. I would prefer a price in the upper $40s. A price of $46.86 would represent a 3.50% yield. Sonoco is a steady performer in a not-so-glamorous business. Simply Safe Dividends gives SON a dividend safety score of 81.
SON's high yield for 2013-2017 ranged from 3.3% in 2017 to 4.1% in 2013. The high yield for 2015 and 2016 was 4.0%. I plan to be patient and watch SON. A 4.0% yield at the current dividend would require a price of $41.00, or a decline of 20.2% from the current price of $51.35.
What's on your watchlist?
I welcome your opinion. Your comments enrich our discussion. I always learn from our Seeking Alpha conversations.
It's not my intent to advocate the purchase or sale of any security. My purpose is to offer ideas for stocks to study and to share a journal of my effort to design and build a retirement portfolio that puts a priority on relative safety, a history of dividend growth and solid future prospects. Your goals and risk tolerance may differ, so please do your own due diligence.
If you are not yet a follower, I invite you to click the "Follow" button at the top of the page. After you click "Follow," you can check "Get Email Alerts," and you will receive an email when an article is published.
